title: Stress, Displacement, and Early‐Life Aging: Telomere Length in Middle Eastern Immigrant and Refugee Mother–Child Dyads
abstract: ABSTRACT Telomere length (TL) is a biomarker of cellular aging and stress exposure. Early‐life TL is linked to long‐term somatic and psychiatric diseases. Children of immigrant and refugee mothers may be vulnerable to biological effects of stress due to maternal psychological distress. This study examined associations between maternal acculturative stress and psychological symptoms (depression and post‐traumatic stress), maternal TL, and child TL in immigrant and refugee Middle Eastern mother–child dyads. In a cross‐sectional design, 6‐ to 24‐month‐old children and their mothers ( N = 165 dyads) were recruited from a Midwestern US community between 2022 and 2024. Maternal psychological distress symptoms were assessed via standardized self‐report measures. Buccal swab samples were collected from mothers and children to measure TL. Multivariate linear regression was used for the analysis. Maternal TL and child gestational age at birth were positively related to child TL. Among immigrant families, higher maternal post‐traumatic stress was significantly related to shorter child TL, whereas for refugee families, higher depressive symptoms were significantly associated with longer child TL. These findings suggest that biological indicators of maternal aging may offer an explanatory power for early‐life stress effects in addition to self‐reported psychological distress.
